questions.q: In Snowsight, what is a dashboard "tile" actually backed by?
options: A static image uploaded by the account administrator
A Snowpipe ingestion job
A worksheet query, whose result set is rendered as a chart or table
A separate, dashboard-only query language distinct from SQL
questions.explain: A tile is a worksheet's query result rendered visually — the same SQL you'd run directly in a worksheet, just saved and displayed on a dashboard.

questions.q: What does this lesson's ACCOUNTADMIN-grants tile query to build its audit trail?
options: The Snowsight UI's audit log download feature
SNOWFLAKE.ACCOUNT_USAGE.QUERY_HISTORY, filtered to successful GRANT statements
A third-party security information and event management (SIEM) export
SNOWFLAKE.ACCOUNT_USAGE.GRANTS_TO_ROLES, which shows only current grants
questions.explain: The tile queries query_history (ACCOUNT_USAGE) for execution_status = 'SUCCESS' and query_type = 'GRANT' matching ACCOUNTADMIN — the history of grant events, not just current state.

questions.q: Per this lesson, how does querying QUERY_HISTORY for GRANT events differ from querying GRANTS_TO_ROLES?
options: QUERY_HISTORY shows the history of grant events over time; GRANTS_TO_ROLES shows the current grant state
They return identical results in every case
GRANTS_TO_ROLES only works for the ACCOUNTADMIN role specifically
QUERY_HISTORY cannot be filtered by query_type
questions.explain: GRANTS_TO_ROLES is a snapshot of who holds what right now; QUERY_HISTORY lets you reconstruct when and by whom a grant was issued — what an audit trail needs.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say a dashboard matters more than a saved query for governance work?
options: Dashboards execute faster than worksheets on the same warehouse
Dashboards automatically grant and revoke privileges based on what they display
It puts multiple signals on one screen, gives a non-SQL reviewer something readable, and turns a check into a standing habit
Dashboards are the only way to query ACCOUNT_USAGE views at all
questions.explain: The lesson lists three concrete reasons: cross-tile pattern visibility, a reviewable artifact for non-technical audiences, and making monitoring a repeated habit rather than a one-off query.

questions.q: What does the "Least Privileged Access: Most Dangerous Person" bar chart in this lesson visualize?
options: The number of tables each user has created
The number of failed login attempts per user
The dollar cost of each user's warehouse usage
Users ranked by their total count of granted privileges, highest first
questions.explain: It's a sorted bar chart of privilege counts per user — turning the question 'who holds too much access?' into something answerable by looking at the top bar.
